extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of science; readers evaluating Bacon's scientific and religious claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for judging Francis Bacon's scientific opinions, experiments, anticipations, and religious views within their historical context; emphasizes distinguishing breadth vs depth, anticipatory insight vs formal discovery, and method-of-arrival vs validity of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider contemporaneous context and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Before casting judgment, consider the circumstances of his age, the attitude of his contemporaries, and the amount of evidence by which the doctrine he rejected was at that time supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Bacon's positions with contemporary opinion and available evidence rather than with later established facts; parallel cases (e.g., resistance to Newton) illustrate that later acceptance does not imply initial error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess author's tone accurately (avoid overstatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept ill-considered characterizations (e.g., that Bacon 'rejected, with the most positive disdain, the system of Copernicus') without checking his actual language and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the original passages (Nov. Org., De Augmentis, Thema Coeli) to judge whether the tone is truly one of 'disdain' or rather of caution/hesitation; quote and compare passages when disputing secondary claims (e.g., Hume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document hesitations and changes over a lifetime
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and trace any wavering or changes in opinion across Bacon's life rather than treating his views as static.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific works and dates (juvenile Praise of Knowledge, Temporis Partus Masculus, Nov. Org., De Augmentis) to show shifts; note that occasional hesitation does not equal final endorsement of the alternative theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish philosopher/amateur role from specialist/discoverer
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Bacon primarily as an interpreter of the philosophy and logic of science (an amateur or dilettante) rather than as a specialist expected to make major original discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust expectations accordingly: value contributions to method, suggestive ideas, and stimulation of inquiry even if he did not produce deep specialist results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance breadth of insight against lack of depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for Bacon's vast range and wealth of illustration while acknowledging that breadth often came at the expense of depth and specialist mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing significance, weigh broad influence and generative suggestions alongside the absence of deep, singular accomplishments in particular branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate anticipation/divination from formal discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Give credit for felicitous anticipations (e.g., attraction, heat as motion) but distinguish these from the later, precise laws and demonstrations constituting true discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether Bacon 'divined' ideas that later were formalized by others (Newton, Tyndall) and avoid conflating prophetic suggestion with having discovered the precise law or proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the sagacity of suggested ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the intellectual insight and prudence of Bacon's suggestions (e.g., on attraction, physical astronomy, instantiae solitariae) as grounds for historical recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the full sections cited (Nov. Org. passages, Instantia Crucis, Descriptio Globi Intellectualis) to see whether the suggestions merit credit for sagacity even if erroneous in details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value advocacy for integrating formal and physical astronomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess Bacon's insistence on connecting calculations (formal astronomy) with philosophical/physical explanations (physical astronomy) as an important methodological stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use his passages (Nov. Org., De Augmentis, Thema Coeli) to judge how strongly he argued for fusion of the two and whether this anticipates later productive approaches (e.g., Newton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge experiments for ingenuity and conclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit originality and intellectual ingenuity of proposed experiments (e.g., hollow lead globe on compressibility of water; experiments on attraction), while noting when they were inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate novelty of experimental conception from the actual validity or conclusiveness (both Bacon's and Accademia del Cimento's experiments were ingenious but inconclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess openness to new theories tempered by scrutiny of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize Bacon's willingness to accept novel theories (e.g., magnetism) but also his justified skepticism when theories rested on complex or arbitrary assumptions (e.g., his attitude to Copernican theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether rejections were dogmatic or methodological—check for concern about arbitrary hypotheses versus empirical fit with phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presentism when judging past scientific positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not ascribe to a past theory the degree of perfection and evidence it later attained; be cautious about retroactive surprise at contemporary resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize the quality of arguments and evidence available at the time; use parallel historical examples (Cartesian adherence, Leibnitz vs Newton) to temper anachronistic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish method-of-arrival from correctness of conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the epistemic status of Bacon's method (e.g., his Method of Exclusion vs comparative tables) from the truth-value of his provisional conclusions (e.g., heat as motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note when a correct conclusion was reached by a non-ideal method; credit the result while qualifying claims about methodological success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh originality against influence and precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming originality, take account of possible predecessors or influences (e.g., Gilbert's influence on Bacon's ideas about attraction or magnetism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give Bacon credit for detaching concepts (e.g., attraction from magnetism) even if the underlying idea had antecedents; cite relevant predecessors and textual references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use careful textual cross-reference to form judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Base conclusions about Bacon's views on a broad set of his writings (Novum Organum, De Augmentis, Sylva Sylvarum, Descriptio Globi Intellectualis, essays, Confession of Faith) and the author's notes; avoid drawing conclusions from isolated passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare multiple passages (references provided throughout the text) and study authorial notes and secondary commentaries (Whewell, Ellis, Herschel, Tyndall) to build a balanced assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Bacon's religious opinions by separating theology and science
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret Bacon's religious statements through his explicit advocacy for separation of theology and natural philosophy; use specified aphorisms and documents as keys to his religious stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the cited references (Nov. Org. i.65, 89; De Augmentis lib. i, iii; Essays on Unity in Religion; Confession of Faith) and avoid over-reading single passages; recognize sincere conviction in fundamental doctrines while noting his methodological separation.
